title: Fire doors
plain: Do crew know where the fire doors are and how they work, and are the doors in good order and never propped open?
why: A fire door that is tied open or damaged lets fire and smoke spread, especially from the engine room to the steering gear.
checks: Sample of fire doors in accommodation, machinery and store spaces
Self-closing doors that close and latch by themselves
No hooks, wedges or tiebacks holding doors open
Condition of door, frame, seals, lock and hinges
Replacement doors match the rating on the Fire Control Plan
ready: Maintenance plan for fire protection systems including fire doors
Records of weekly, quarterly and annual fire door tests
Fire Control Plan showing door ratings
Company procedure with test frequency for fire doors
Doors clear of obstructions
traps: Engine room to steering gear door tied open
Hold-back hooks, wedges or ropes on self-closing doors
Self-closing device does not fully close or latch
Corrosion, gaps, punctures or damaged packing
Cables passed through the door or frame
Records say tested but the door is defective
say: Our fire doors are listed in the maintenance plan and tested at the intervals in our SMS. I can show you the records and the Fire Control Plan. Doors that must self-close are never held open, and any defect is reported and repaired straight away.

practice.q: Where are the fire doors in the machinery space and what are they for?
a: Name the main locations from the Fire Control Plan
They stop fire and smoke spreading between spaces
They must be kept closed or self-closing

practice.q: How do you test the fire doors and how often?
a: Weekly check of control panel indicators
Quarterly local operation test of main vertical zone doors
Annual test of remote release, all recorded

practice.q: Can you hold this self-closing door open while working?
a: No, no tiebacks, hooks or wedges
Only approved fail-safe hold-back with remote release

tip: Check the engine room and steering gear doors on your rounds and take out any wedge or rope you find. Inspectors look there first.

title: Firefighter's outfits and SCBA
plain: Do crew know where the firefighter's outfits and breathing apparatus are, how to use them, and are they ready to use?
why: Fire and enclosed space rescue depend on breathing apparatus that works and people who can put it on correctly.
checks: Outfit storage areas and the outfits ready for immediate use
Inventory and condition of one selected outfit
SCBA fully charged with the right number of full spare bottles
Harness and facemask laid out for quick donning
Demonstration of donning, leak test, mask seal test and low air alarm
ready: Maintenance plan including outfits, SCBA and compressor
Records of monthly outfit checks and weekly and annual SCBA checks
Five-year hydrostatic test records for cylinders
Compressor usage log and air quality test records
Company procedure for use and maintenance of outfits and SCBA
traps: Outfits or SCBA not in the place shown on the fire plan
Outfit incomplete or any item defective
Cylinder not fully charged or spare bottles missing
Cylinders not interchangeable or not pressure tested on time
Officer cannot explain cylinder endurance, filling pressure or compressor use
Safety lamps not explosion proof, or not enough intrinsically safe radios for the fire teams
Crew cannot don the SCBA and do the safety checks
say: Our outfits and SCBA are kept ready in the locations on the fire plan and checked as set out in our maintenance plan. I can show the records, the compressor log and air quality results. I can also don the set and carry out the leak, mask seal and low air alarm checks.

practice.q: Please put on the SCBA and do the checks before entering.
a: Check cylinder pressure and open valve
Test mask seal on the face

practice.q: How do you refill the bottles and keep the air safe?
a: Use the compressor following the procedure
Log usage and test air quality at the set interval
Follow instructions to avoid overfilling bottles of different pressure

practice.q: How long does a full cylinder last and who checks the sets?
a: State the endurance for our sets
Checks follow the maintenance plan and are recorded
Defects fixed promptly, bottles recharged after use

tip: Practise donning with a stopwatch and a partner. Know your cylinder endurance and filling pressure by heart, as officers are asked.

title: Fire hoses, nozzles and international shore connection
plain: Do crew know the fire hoses, nozzles and shore connection, and are they complete, working and ready for immediate use?
why: In a fire you need water now, so missing hose parts or a shore connection without bolts can cost the ship.
checks: Random hoses and nozzles in accommodation, machinery spaces and main deck
Washers, spanners, couplings and nozzle jet and spray controls
Hydrant washers and connections
International shore connection with nuts, bolts, gasket and two spanners
Rating questioned on purpose and operation
ready: Maintenance plan covering hoses, nozzles and shore connection
Records of monthly, quarterly and annual checks
Fire Control Plan showing hose locations
Procedure with test frequency, hose pressure test and replacement criteria
Shore connection stowed ready and clearly marked
traps: Hoses or nozzles missing from the places on the fire plan
Shore connection missing bolts, nuts, washers, gasket or spanners
Hose shorter than 10 m or longer than allowed for its location
Leaking, worn or defective hoses and couplings
Rating cannot explain what the shore connection is for
Records incomplete or not matching the equipment
say: Hoses and nozzles are in the places shown on the Fire Control Plan and checked under our maintenance plan. The international shore connection is marked, protected and complete with bolts, gasket and spanners. I can show the records and demonstrate the equipment.

practice.q: What is the international shore connection and where is it?
a: Standard flange that links shore fire main to ship's hydrant
Say where it is stowed and that it can be used on either side

practice.q: What should be with the shore connection?
How do you check a fire hose and nozzle?
a: Nozzle jet and spray control works

tip: Hoses laid out for cargo or bunkering should be back at their locations at other times. Ratings should know the shore connection by sight.

title: Portable fire extinguishers
plain: Are portable extinguishers in the right places, charged, clearly marked and understood by the crew?
why: A small fire is stopped by a working extinguisher in the first minute, if people know which one to use.
checks: Sample of each type of extinguisher
Required markings, last annual service date and last ship check date
Position matches the Fire Control Plan
Spare charges or spare extinguishers inventory
One officer or rating explains how a chosen extinguisher works
ready: Fire Control Plan
Maintenance plan including extinguishers
Inspection and service records, annual service at intervals not over one year
Inventory of spare charges or extinguishers
Company procedure for maintenance including service agents
traps: Extinguisher missing or not where the fire plan shows
Not fully charged or not ready for use
Markings or instructions unreadable or missing
No date of last onboard check or annual service
Not enough spare charges
Fire plan distribution does not meet the number rules for ships built from 1 January 2009
Crew unfamiliar with using the extinguisher
say: Our extinguishers are placed as on the Fire Control Plan, checked by the crew and serviced at intervals not over one year. Each one carries its instructions and service dates. I can show the records and the spares inventory.

practice.q: Which extinguisher would you use on this type of fire and how do you operate it?
a: Match type to the fire using the marking
Pull pin, aim at base, squeeze

practice.q: How do you know this extinguisher is in good order?
a: Gauge or weight and seal check
Dates of last ship check and annual service

practice.q: How do you manage spares?
a: Inventory of spare charges or units

tip: After any use or drill, recharge or replace the extinguisher as soon as possible and update the inventory. Check tags have both dates.

title: Emergency Escape Breathing Devices (EEBDs)
plain: Do crew know where the EEBDs are and what they are for, and are they in date, marked and ready?
why: EEBDs give a few minutes of air to escape smoke or gas, but only if they are in the right place and not expired.
checks: Sample EEBDs in machinery spaces, pumproom and accommodation
Position matches the Fire Control Plan
Expiry date, pressure and readable donning instructions
Required markings on each unit
Two ratings asked about location and purpose
ready: Company procedure on use, number, location and training of EEBDs
Inspection and maintenance records in the maintenance plan
Spare EEBDs as shown on the Fire Control Plan
Hydrostatic test records for rechargeable cylinders
Training units clearly marked
traps: EEBDs not where the fire control plan shows them
Fewer spares than the plan says
Past expiry date or cylinder pressure out of range
Donning instructions unreadable
Missing marking of serial number, trademark, shelf life or approval
Training units not clearly marked
Rechargeable cylinders not hydrostatically tested on time
say: Our EEBDs are placed as shown on the fire plan and checked under our procedure. Each is in date, marked and has readable instructions. They are only for escape, not firefighting, and crew are trained to put them on before leaving a space.

practice.q: Where is the nearest EEBD and when do you use it?
a: Point out the location from the plan
Use it to escape a hazardous atmosphere
Don it before leaving the space

practice.q: Can you use an EEBD for firefighting or entering a tank?
a: Use SCBA for firefighting or oxygen deficient spaces

practice.q: How do you check the EEBDs?

tip: Hang a quick check tag on each EEBD showing the date. Show crew how long the device lasts, at least 10 minutes by guideline.

title: Wheeled (mobile) fire extinguishers
plain: Do engineers know the wheeled extinguishers, and are they in place, charged, marked and ready?
why: Wheeled units are the main tool against an engine room oil fire before the fixed system is used.
checks: All wheeled extinguishers in the machinery spaces
Required marking, annual service date and last ship check date
Position matches the Fire Control Plan
Inventory of spare charges
Engineer officer or rating asked how to operate one
ready: Fire Control Plan
Maintenance plan with monthly, annual, five-yearly and ten-yearly items
Records of inspections, tests and servicing
Inventory of spare charges
Instructions readable on each unit
traps: Unit not fully charged or not ready to use
Missing or not at the plan location
Markings or service dates missing
Not included in the maintenance plan
Not enough spare charges
Records incomplete or not matching condition
Engineer cannot explain how to operate it
say: Our wheeled extinguishers are in the engine room as shown on the fire plan and are checked monthly and serviced as in the maintenance plan. I can show the records and the spare charges list, and I can operate the unit.

practice.q: How do you use this wheeled extinguisher?
a: Wheel to the fire, unreel hose
Direct at base of fire from a safe distance

practice.q: What checks are done and how often?
a: Five-yearly and ten-yearly tests including hydrostatic

practice.q: What spares do you carry?

tip: If the ship has no wheeled extinguishers, this question is marked not answerable, so know whether yours are fitted.

title: Davit-launched lifeboats, release gear and launching appliances
plain: Do officers know how the lifeboats, release gear and davits work, and are they in good order with inspection and test records?
why: Poor maintenance of survival craft has caused many accidents, so the boat must work when needed.
checks: Company procedure for periodic inspection and testing
Weekly, monthly, annual and five-yearly records
Lifting hooks and keel structure free of corrosion
Engine started with propeller shown moving ahead and astern
Officer explains items from the SOLAS III/36 monthly checklist
ready: Monthly inspection checklist and weekly records
Annual and five-yearly thorough examination reports
Maintenance manuals for boats and davits on board
Bridge Log Book entries
Records for fall renewal
traps: Records of weekly, monthly, annual or five-yearly checks incomplete
Falls in service longer than five years
No clear on-load release instructions or release control not in contrasting colour
Engine will not start or no engine instructions near the controls
Missing or badly stowed equipment
Davit limit switches stuck, gearcase breather blocked or painted over
Boat, davit or locations not marked with required symbols
say: Our lifeboats and davits are inspected weekly and monthly under our SMS, with annual and five-yearly examinations by authorised service providers. I can show the checklists and records, start the engine and explain the monthly checks and the release gear.

practice.q: Start the lifeboat engine and show ahead and astern.
a: Engage the gear, check propeller turns both ways

practice.q: Explain the on-load and off-load release.
a: Two release capabilities, normal and on-load
Green means reset, red means danger
Know the safety steps before using on-load

practice.q: When were the falls last renewed?
a: Inspect falls and gripes for condition

tip: Check the gearcase breather vent and limit switches each month. Painted-over vents are a classic finding.

title: Free-fall lifeboat, release systems and launching appliance
plain: Do officers know the free-fall lifeboat and its release and recovery gear, and is it in good order with records?
why: A free-fall boat only helps if its release, ramp and restraints are ready and safe when the crew abandon ship.
checks: Company procedure for inspection and testing
Boat, equipment and release system against the monthly checklist
Launching, recovery and stowage systems
Engine started with propeller shown moving ahead and astern
Officer explains items from the monthly checklist
ready: SOLAS III/36 monthly checklist
Weekly and monthly inspection records
Annual and five-yearly thorough examination reports
Bridge Log Book
Maintenance manuals on board
traps: Records incomplete or checklist missing
Falls in service more than five years
Release not protected against accidental release or not in a contrasting colour
Seat harnesses not in good order
Safety or maintenance chains or pins left in place
Hydraulic hoses, rollers or skid ramp in poor condition
Boat not properly secured in stowed position
Engine would not start
say: Our free-fall lifeboat is checked under our SMS with weekly, monthly, annual and five-yearly records. Safety pins are removed after checks so it is ready to launch. I can show the checklist, start the engine and explain the release system.

practice.q: What do you do after recovering or testing the boat?
a: Leave it ready for immediate launch
Remove safety and maintenance chains and pins

practice.q: How is the release protected from accidental release?
What do you check on the ramp and launching gear?
a: Recovery limit switches and securing means

tip: Make a pre-inspection routine: pins out, harnesses checked, rollers free. Keep it written on the checklist.

title: Dedicated rescue boat and launching appliance
plain: Do officers know the rescue boat and its davit, and are they in good order with inspection and test records?
why: The rescue boat must be ready at once to recover a person, with an engine that starts and a davit that works.
checks: Company procedure for inspection and testing
Records of periodic inspections and tests
Engine started and drive engaged
Davit slewed manually and by reserve power
Officer explains operation, inspection and testing
ready: Weekly and monthly inspection checklist
Annual and five-yearly examination records
Full maintenance manuals on board
Bridge Log Book
Rescue boat equipment complete and stowed
traps: Records of checks incomplete
Manuals for boat and davit not on board
Emergency repair to inflatable still pending permanent repair
Inflatable not fully inflated, not in continuous readiness
Engine will not start or no starting instructions near controls
Davit cannot be slewed manually or by reserve power
No checklist or missing symbols marking
say: Our rescue boat is kept ready, inspected and tested under our SMS, with annual and five-yearly service by authorised providers. I can show records, start the engine, engage the drive and slew the davit by hand and reserve power.

practice.q: Show me how you start the rescue boat engine.
How do you slew the davit without main power?
a: By hand or reserve power as per instructions

practice.q: What if the inflatable boat has a repair?
a: Permanent repair at an approved service station
Emergency repair is not acceptable long term

tip: Practise the manual slew regularly. It is the step crews forget.

title: Rocket parachute flares and line throwing appliances
plain: Do officers know where the flares and line throwing gear are and how they work, and are they in date and ready?
why: Distress flares and line throwers are used when seconds matter, so they must be complete, in date and stowed on the bridge.
checks: Stowage place on or near the bridge
Flares and line throwing appliances for number and condition
Expiry dates of flares, rockets and lines
Rockets and lines stowed together and ready
Officer explains purpose, use and inspection
ready: Company procedure for periodic inspection
Inspection records
Stowage marked with LSA symbol and number of devices
Table of life-saving signals on the bridge
Waterproof and weatherproof stowage
traps: Fewer than 12 rocket parachute flares or no line throwing appliance
Not stowed on or near the bridge
Stowage not marked with symbols and number
Stowage not weatherproof
No brief operating instructions on the items
Any item past expiry date
Rockets and lines stowed apart
No table of life-saving signals on the bridge
say: Flares and the line throwing appliance are stowed on the bridge, marked with the correct symbols and checked under our SMS. All items are in date and the line throwing set is assembled and ready. A table of life-saving signals is on the bridge.

practice.q: How many parachute flares must you carry and where?
a: On or near the navigation bridge

practice.q: How do you use the line throwing appliance?
a: Follow the instructions on the unit

practice.q: Where are the life-saving signals?
a: Available to the officer of the watch

tip: Put a list of expiry dates on the stowage door and check it at each monthly inspection.

title: Liferafts, hydrostatic releases and liferaft launching appliances
plain: Do officers know the liferafts, hydrostatic releases and davits, and are they stowed, serviced and ready to use?
why: Liferafts must float free and be ready within minutes, and servicing or release units out of date can fail them.
checks: Company procedure and servicing records from approved station
Liferafts stowed and ready for immediate release
Hydrostatic releases rigged as per manufacturer and in date
Painters attached permanently to the ship
Officer explains operation, inspection and testing
ready: Servicing certificates for rafts and release units
Weekly and monthly inspection records
Bridge Log Book
Embarkation ladders in good condition with handholds
Lighting and lifejackets for remote rafts
traps: Not enough liferaft capacity for everyone on board
Raft not in continuous readiness
Painter not permanently attached to ship
Hydrostatic release rigged wrongly, unmarked or past expiry
Raft or release not serviced at the required interval
Embarkation ladder missing or poor, no handholds
Remote raft without lights or means of embarkation
Battery lamps without recent proof of three hours of light
say: Our liferafts and hydrostatic releases are serviced by an authorised station at the required intervals and checked onboard weekly and monthly. Painters are attached, releases are rigged to the manufacturer's instructions, and I can show the certificates and records.

practice.q: How does the hydrostatic release work and when does it expire?
a: Releases the raft automatically at depth

practice.q: How are the liferafts stowed?
a: Ready for release one at a time

practice.q: What is needed for a remotely stowed raft?
a: Embarkation ladder, not a knotted rope

tip: If rafts have an extended service interval with an onboard kit, have the flag acceptance and training evidence ready.

title: Lifebuoys, lights, smoke floats and lifelines
plain: Are lifebuoys, their lights, smoke floats and lines in good order, clearly marked and placed correctly around the ship?
why: A person overboard needs a lifebuoy within reach on either side, with a light by night and a line where needed.
checks: Number of lifebuoys and spread on both sides, each open deck and near the stern
Lights, smoke floats and buoyant lifelines
Stowage marked with symbols and lifebuoys marked with ship name and port
Retro-reflective tape and quick release freedom
Monthly checklist and log
ready: Company procedure for lifebuoys and associated gear
Monthly inspection checklist and log records
Battery-type self-igniting lights
Smoke floats in date with free quick release from the bridge
Marking of any non-intrinsically safe lights
traps: Fewer lifebuoys than required
Too few lifebuoys with lights
A lifebuoy fitted with both a light and a lifeline
No buoyant lifeline of the right length on each side
Lifebuoys lashed in brackets or not marked with name and port
Retro-reflective tape missing
Smoke float expired, stuck release, or its lifebuoy under 4 kg
Non-intrinsically safe light inside the gas hazardous area
say: Our lifebuoys are spread on both sides and near the stern, free to cast loose and marked with the ship's name and port. Lights, smoke floats and lifelines are checked monthly and recorded under our SMS. Non-intrinsically safe lights are controlled so they stay out of gas zones.

practice.q: Which lifebuoys have lights, lifelines and smoke floats?
a: Lifelines on at least one each side
At least half have self-igniting lights
Smoke floats on bridge release, not on lifeline buoys

practice.q: How do you keep non-intrinsically safe lights out of the cargo area?
a: Use only intrinsically safe lights in the hazardous area

practice.q: What is checked at the monthly inspection?
a: Lights, smoke float expiry and quick release

tip: Tag the non-intrinsically safe lights clearly and check each month that none has moved to the tank deck.

title: Immersion suits
plain: Do crew know the immersion suits, and are they in good order, easy to reach and clearly shown on the ship?
why: In cold water an immersion suit protects against hypothermia, so it must fit, be undamaged and be quick to put on.
checks: Suits at one stowage place and sight of other places
Monthly inspection and air-pressure test records
Suit size and type match the storage bag
Zips, seams, tape, whistles and lights
An officer or rating shows donning
ready: Company procedure with number, type, sizes and location of suits
Records of monthly inspections
Records of air-pressure tests at intervals not over three years, or more often for suits over ten years old
Stowage marked with symbols and number of suits
Suits at the forward liferaft or other remote location
traps: No suit of the right size for each person
Stowage not marked with symbols and number
No suits at the remote liferaft location
Donning instructions unreadable
Bag label does not match the suit inside
Failed seams, stuck zips or damaged tape
Whistle or light missing, or battery out of date
Vacuum-packed suits with damaged packing and no loose suits for training
say: Our immersion suits are stowed and marked as in our SMS, with the right sizes for everyone. We inspect them monthly and air-pressure test them at the intervals we have set. I can show the records and put on a suit myself.

practice.q: Show me how to put on an immersion suit.
a: Unpack and don it without help
Zip fully and check hood and gloves
Know the suit is worn with a lifejacket if marked

practice.q: How do you inspect the suits monthly?
a: Dry inside and out, no damage, zip easy
Tape, whistle, light and battery date

practice.q: How are vacuum-packed suits handled?
a: Damaged pack is treated as non vacuum-packed

tip: Use the monthly check as a donning practice for new joiners, and put the air-pressure test dates on a wall chart.

title: Lifejackets and personal flotation devices (PFDs)
plain: Do crew know the lifejackets and working lifejackets, and are they in good condition, easy to reach and maintained?
why: A lifejacket that is missing, damaged or out of reach, or not worn for work over the side, can turn a fall into a death.
checks: Lifejackets at one stowage place and sight of others
Company procedures including working lifejackets
Sample of working lifejackets
Monthly inspection and inflatable annual service records
Rating asked about use of working lifejackets
ready: Company procedure for lifejackets and working lifejackets
Monthly inspection records
Annual service records for inflatable lifejackets if carried
Marked stowage with symbols and numbers
Extra lifejackets on bridge, ECR, forward raft and other watch stations
traps: No procedure for working lifejackets
Lifejackets not suited to the type of lifeboat
Stowage not marked with symbols and number
Not enough on bridge, engine room or forward liferaft
Retro-reflective tape, whistles or lights missing or out of date
Buoyant line or lifting means missing or defective
Inflatable not serviced annually
No working lifejackets for overside or exposed work
say: Lifejackets are stowed and marked for everyone, with extra sets at watch stations and remote craft. We check them monthly and service inflatables as required. Working lifejackets are used for overside and exposed work as in our SMS.

practice.q: When must a working lifejacket be worn?
a: Work overside or in an exposed position
Risk of falling or being washed overboard
Work in or from a ship's boat

practice.q: What do you check on a lifejacket?
a: Buoyant line, lifting means and general condition

practice.q: How often are inflatable lifejackets serviced?

tip: Hang working lifejackets near the work area and brief ratings at toolbox talks. Ratings are interviewed on this.
refs: MCA Code of Safe Working Practices

title: Emergency lighting
plain: Do officers know how emergency lighting is tested and maintained, is testing recorded, and does the system work?
why: If the main power fails, emergency lights guide people to muster stations, boats and escape routes.
checks: Company procedure for inspection and testing of emergency lighting
Test records against the procedure
Demonstration of the emergency lighting
Sample of emergency lights working
Lighting for the water where survival craft launch
ready: Procedure stating instructions, frequency and recording
Records of weekly testing
Location of the switches for the emergency lighting
Clean and dry emergency light fittings
Lighting over the side at boats and remote liferaft
traps: No procedure for testing
Procedure does not require testing at least weekly
Records missing or not matching the procedure
Responsible officer does not know the procedure
Officer does not know where the emergency light switches are
Lights not working, dirty or full of water
Lighting of the launch water area in poor condition
say: Our SMS requires emergency lighting to be tested weekly and recorded. I know where the switches are and can demonstrate the system. Defective or dirty lights are reported and fixed.

practice.q: How often do you test the emergency lighting?
a: At least once a week by our procedure
Also tested at abandon ship drills

practice.q: Where are the switches for the emergency lighting?
a: Know what comes on and for how long

practice.q: What areas need emergency light?
a: Muster and embarkation stations and over the side
Alleyways, machinery spaces and steering gear

tip: While testing, walk the ship and note dirty or flooded fittings at the same time. It is easy to fix and often found.

title: Enclosed space entry procedures
plain: Do crew know the enclosed space entry procedure, and can you show every entry followed it strictly?
why: People die in enclosed spaces from low oxygen or toxic gas, so entry must be controlled every time.
checks: Company procedure and the list of spaces needing a permit
At least two permits from different space types
Risk assessment, validity not over 12 hours, atmosphere tests, isolation
Signatures by master or responsible person, attendant, entrants and supervisor
A rating asked about their role and signing the permit
ready: Enclosed space entry procedure and space categorisation
Entry permits from the last six months for deck and engine spaces
Pumproom and similar room entry records for the last two months
Bridge Log Book and planned maintenance system
Rescue and resuscitation equipment in good condition
traps: No procedure, or not all enclosed spaces identified
No risk assessment before each entry
Permit missing, incomplete or approved by the person entering
Not all gases tested that suit the previous contents
No record of blanking or isolation of pipes and power
Cargo tank entered without cleaning as per procedure
Breathing sets used routinely instead of cleaning and gas freeing
No gas readings or entry and exit times for pumproom entry without a permit
Personal multi-gas detectors not required
say: No one enters an enclosed space without our permit or the documented alternative process. We risk assess, ventilate, test the atmosphere, isolate and brief before each entry. I can show recent permits and explain each person's role.

practice.q: What readings must you have before entry?
a: Oxygen 21 percent, do not enter if lower until the cause is found and resolved
Flammable vapour below 1 percent of LFL
Toxic gases no more than 50 percent of OEL

practice.q: How long is a permit valid?
a: Valid only while conditions are met

practice.q: As an attendant, what is your job?
a: Raise the alarm and do not enter to rescue

tip: Check that the person who approves the permit is never the person entering. Keep two months of pumproom logs handy.

title: Hot work procedure
plain: Do crew know the hot work procedure, and can you show all hot work was done by the procedure and with a permit?
why: Sparks and heat on a tanker can ignite gas, oil or cargo, so hot work must be tightly controlled.
checks: Company hot work procedure
Up to two recent permits with risk assessment, work plan and planning meeting
Shore management approval where required
Instructions posted in the designated hot work space
No undocumented hot work seen during the inspection
ready: Hot work procedure in line with ISGOTT Chapter 9
Hot work permits from the last six months with risk assessments and work plans
Records of planning meetings and shore approvals
Posted instructions in the workshop or designated space
Shield or curtain for the designated space
traps: No hot work procedure or not matching ISGOTT Chapter 9
Hot work outside the designated space without a permit
Permit without risk assessment, work plan or planning meeting
Shore approval missing where the procedure needs it
Master or responsible officer approval missing
No instructions posted in the designated space
Instructions do not say when, who, shield or Master permission
Engine rating cannot explain the instructions
say: All hot work outside our designated space is under a permit, with a risk assessment, work plan and planning meeting. In the workshop we follow the posted instructions, use a shield and get the Master's or responsible officer's permission first. Hot work stops during bunkering, cargo operations and tank cleaning.

practice.q: What counts as hot work?
a: Welding, cutting, burning, gouging, heating, soldering
Power tools, non-intrinsically safe electronics and combustion engines in a hazardous area
If the SMS has no guidance, work is prohibited

practice.q: When is hot work not allowed in the designated space?
a: During crude oil washing and tank cleaning

practice.q: What approval is needed for hot work in a hazardous area?
a: Hot work plan and risk assessment
Shore management approval and a permit approved onboard

tip: Remember the fire alarm: cover or isolate the smoke detector only as the procedure says, and restore it after.

title: Working at height
plain: Do crew know the working at height procedure, and is a permit or risk assessment used every time?
why: Falls from height are a leading cause of serious injury and death at sea.
checks: Company procedure with the height that triggers controls
Recent permits or risk assessments match the real job and are approved correctly
Inventory and periodic checks of harnesses and equipment
Sample of PPE and equipment condition
Rating questioned on the procedure and permit process
ready: Working at height procedure
Permits or risk assessments for the last two months
Inventory and periodic inspection records of PPE and equipment
Harnesses, lifelines, fall arresters, bosun's chairs, stages in good condition
Checks before each use, as the procedure requires
traps: No procedure that covers working at height
No permit or risk assessment where one was needed
Permit does not fit the actual job or ship
Approved at the wrong level
No inventory or periodic check records
PPE or equipment in poor condition
Officer or rating unfamiliar with the procedure
say: Before any work at height, we do a risk assessment or permit as our SMS requires, approved at the right level. Harnesses and equipment are checked before every use and periodically, and the records are here. Everyone doing the job knows the controls.

practice.q: From what height do your controls apply?
a: State the height in our SMS
Check any exclusions in the procedure

practice.q: What do you check before using a harness or bosun's chair?
Who approves the permit?
a: The level named in our procedure

tip: Make sure the permit describes the job being done today, not a copied one from last month.
refs: MCA Code of Safe Working Practices Ch 17

title: Working over the side
plain: Do crew know the over-the-side work procedure, and are standard procedures, permits or risk assessments used every time?
why: A person who falls overboard may not be seen or recovered, so work over the side needs strict control.
checks: Company procedure including the ban on working over the side underway
Standard procedures for ladder and gangway rigging
Recent permits or risk assessments match the real work
Inventory and checks of PPE and equipment
Deck rating asked about rigging ladders underway and supervision
ready: Working over the side procedure
Standard work procedures for combination ladder, accommodation ladder and gangway
Permits or risk assessments from the last six months
Records of periodic checks of PPE and equipment
Lifejackets, lifelines, harnesses and fall arresters in good order
traps: No procedure that covers working over the side
No permit or risk assessment and no standard procedure
Permit does not match the real work
Approval at the wrong level
No inventory or checks of equipment
Equipment in poor condition
Rating cannot explain supervision on deck and bridge while underway
say: We do not work over the side while underway except in defined cases such as rigging a ladder or boat exercises. Those have a standard procedure or a permit, lifejackets, lines and supervision on deck and bridge. Boats are ready, and equipment is checked and recorded.

practice.q: When can work over the side be done underway?
a: Only in defined cases, such as rigging ladders or boat drills
Under a standard procedure or permit
Rescue boat ready and watcher in place

practice.q: What protection do you wear when rigging a pilot ladder?
a: Safety line or fall prevention device and harness
Supervision on deck and bridge informed

practice.q: What does the bridge need to do while ladder work is going on underway?
a: Keep supervision as per our procedure
Know engine status and speed limit

tip: Brief deck ratings on the standard procedure for ladder rigging. Interviewers often ask about it.
refs: MCA Code of Safe Working Practices Ch 10

title: Working on electrical equipment and systems
plain: Do officers know the electrical work procedure, and are permits or risk assessments used every time electrical work is done?
why: Electric shock can kill at low voltage on board, and a wrong isolation can kill or ignite gas.
checks: Company procedure for electrical work
At least two recent permits or risk assessments match the job
Notices on treatment of electric shock in spaces with switchgear
Planned maintenance system and daily planning records
Electrician or engineer asked about high voltage, live work and hazardous areas
ready: Electrical work procedure with general and high voltage definitions
Permits or risk assessments from the last two months
Electric shock treatment notices posted
Insulating mats, gloves and PPE checked
Supervision records where the procedure requires them
traps: No procedure covering electrical work
No permit or risk assessment required or completed
Permit does not fit the job or is approved at the wrong level
No documented supervision where the procedure needs it
Electric shock notices missing
Electrician unfamiliar with high voltage, live work, test bench or hazardous area controls
say: Electrical work follows our SMS, with a permit or risk assessment and isolation before work starts. Extra controls apply to high voltage, live work, test benches and hazardous areas. Electric shock treatment notices are posted in switchgear spaces.

practice.q: How do you make equipment safe before you work on it?
a: Remove fuses or open breakers, lock open if possible
Permit and competent person in charge

practice.q: What extra controls apply to high voltage work?
a: Approval at the level set in the procedure

practice.q: What PPE do you use?
a: Eye protection, no metal fittings or jewellery

tip: If no electrical permit was done in the last two months, be ready to say when the last one was.
refs: MCA Code of Safe Working Practices Ch 20

title: Control of hazardous energy
plain: Do officers know how hazardous energy is identified and isolated before work, and is it documented every time?
why: Stored pressure, power or stuck valves can injure people or spill pollution if not isolated and checked first.
checks: Company control of hazardous energy procedure
At least two permits or risk assessments showing isolation points
Planned maintenance tasks that need isolation have the paperwork
LO/TO equipment fitted has a matching permit and inventory exists
Officer explains how zero energy is verified
ready: Hazardous energy and LO/TO procedure
Permits or risk assessments from the last three months
Daily work planning records and logbooks
Inventory of LO/TO equipment
Training records for people doing isolations
traps: No procedure and no LO/TO equipment
No inventory of LO/TO equipment
Work done with no documented energy control
Locks or tags on equipment but no permit or reason
Permit lists isolation points that were not locked or tagged
Machinery opened with no isolation at all
Officer cannot explain zero energy verification
say: Before work, we identify energy sources such as pressure, electrical or stored energy, and isolate them with lock-out and tag-out. We verify a zero energy state independently and record it on the permit. After work we reinstate and test.

practice.q: What counts as hazardous energy?
a: Pressure in pipes or air reservoirs, electrical stored energy
Hydrostatic pressure on sea valves, gravity, heat and motion

practice.q: How do you know the system is safe to open?
a: If not possible, stop and re-assess

practice.q: Who can do and check the isolation?
a: Approved on the permit by the authorised person

tip: Match every lock or tag on board to a permit. A tag with no paperwork is a finding.

title: Portable and personal gas measurement instruments
plain: Do officers know the gas meters, and are there enough, working, tested and calibrated on time?
why: Gas readings decide whether people can safely enter a space or handle cargo, so the meters must be right.
checks: Company procedure for operation, testing and calibration
Instruments, spare parts, test gases and tubes or chips
Sampling hoses long enough for the deepest tank
Inventory, test and calibration records, disposable monitor start dates
Officer demonstrates the pre-use accuracy test
ready: Procedure for testing, calibration and maintenance
Inventory of instruments, spares, test gases and consumables
Manuals in the working language of the ship
Test and calibration records
Commissioning dates for disposable personal monitors
traps: Fewer than two instruments measuring oxygen, LFL, H2S and CO
No means to measure toxic gases of the cargoes carried
Not enough or expired tubes or chips
Sampling hose too short for the deepest tank
No oxygen and hydrocarbon meter for inert atmosphere on IG or nitrogen ships
Wrong or insufficient test gas, or wrong gas used
Calibration and testing records missing
Disposable monitors used past expiry or start date not recorded
Manuals not in working language
say: We carry at least two instruments for oxygen, LFL, H2S and CO plus means for cargo toxic gases and inert gas. They are tested and calibrated per the SMS and manufacturer, with records. I can show the inventory and do the pre-use accuracy test.

practice.q: How do you test the gas meter before use?
How often are the instruments tested?
a: Tested with test gas at least monthly or after any fault

practice.q: What are the limits of your instruments?
a: Sensor type and what it can measure
Whether usable in inert atmosphere or above atmospheric pressure

tip: Defective meters marked out of service and reported are not a finding if you still have enough working ones. Mark them clearly.

title: Testing double-hull and double bottom spaces for flammable gas
plain: Do deck officers know how double-hull and double bottom spaces are tested for flammable gas, with records to show it?
why: Gas in ballast or void spaces next to cargo tanks is an early sign of a leak or structural crack.
checks: Company procedure for method and frequency of monitoring
Records of gas measurements in double hull, double bottom and void spaces
Fixed system sensors isolated only in line with ballast level
Manual readings where a sensor was isolated
Alarm set not above 30 percent LFL and calibration records
ready: Procedure describing monitoring, recording and action if gas is found
Portable meter readings log
Records of fixed system operation and sensor isolation times
Sensor calibration records
Incident reports for any gas detected
traps: No procedure with method and frequency
Deck officer does not know the procedure
No or incomplete gas measurement records
Fixed sensors isolated with no manual readings
Fixed system defective, uncalibrated or alarm set wrongly
No working portable flammable gas meter
Flammable gas detected from a structural defect within the last 12 months
say: Our procedure sets how often we test the double-hull, double bottom and void spaces and how we record the results. Where the fixed system sensors are isolated for ballast, we take manual readings. I can show the logs, alarm settings and calibration records.

practice.q: How do you monitor these spaces?
What if the fixed system is out of order?
What do you do if gas is found?
a: Investigate for leak or structural defect

tip: Write the sensor isolation and reconnection times in the log each time ballast is moved.

title: Fixed gas detection systems required by the IGC Code
plain: Do officers know the fixed gas detection system, and is it working, maintained and calibrated with correct alarm settings?
why: On gas carriers early detection of a leak prevents vapour cloud fires and asphyxiation.
checks: Company procedure for operation and maintenance
Central control station: all sensors monitored, no faults, normal readings
Alarm set points match the IGC Code, company procedure and the cargo carried
Calibration data, calibration gases and equipment
Portable detectors listed for IGC Code and toxic gas records if used
ready: Procedure with calibration, alarm test and shutdown test frequencies
List of sensors with alarm and shutdown set points
Manufacturer's calibration instructions
Calibration gas inventory in date and correct type
Maintenance plan records and toxic gas monitoring records
traps: No procedure for the fixed system
Not all sensors monitored, system fault or defective sensor showing
Set points not as required or not changed for the cargo carried
Sensors not calibrated as manufacturer and company require
Wrong or expired calibration gas, or missing calibration equipment
Sealed cabinet for gas detection equipment open or not sealable
Portable detectors required by the Code missing
Maintenance plan missing the gas system or calibrations
say: Our fixed gas detection monitors all sensors with no faults showing. Alarm and shutdown points follow the IGC Code and are set for the cargo on board. I can show calibration records and in-date calibration gas.

practice.q: What alarm level do sensors in inert spaces use?
a: Set to the equivalent of 30 percent LFL in air

practice.q: How do you calibrate the sensors?
a: Follow manufacturer's instructions and company frequency
Use correct in-date gas and equipment
Record results and confirm set points

practice.q: Where do alarms sound?

tip: Change set points when you change cargo grade and write it in the log. Inspectors check this.

title: Fixed gas detection system required by the IGF Code
plain: Do officers know the fixed gas detection for gas-fuelled systems, and is it working, calibrated and maintained?
why: A leak from the gas or low-flashpoint fuel system must be caught fast to protect the ship and crew.
checks: Company procedure for operation and testing
Central control station fully working with no faults
Alarm set point for a selected sensor matches the IGF Code
Calibration and shutdown test records at the set frequency
Calibration gas meets the manufacturer's specification
ready: Procedure defining calibration, set point checks, alarm tests and shutdown tests
Manufacturer's instruction manual
Maintenance plan with frequencies
Calibration and test records
In-date calibration gas
traps: No procedure for the system
Maintenance plan without the system or without frequencies
Officer does not know calibration or shutdown test tasks
Sensors not calibrated per the plan
Calibration gas out of date or not to specification
Bridge or control room alarms not tested
Alarm or shutdown set points not per the IGF Code
Sensors out of service, inhibited or disconnected
say: Our system is covered by a company procedure and the maintenance plan with calibration and shutdown test frequencies. Alarms are checked on the bridge or control station and calibration gas is in date. I can show records and the set points.

practice.q: What are the alarm and shutdown set points?
a: Alarm at 20 percent of lower explosion limit
Safety system at 40 percent at two detectors
Ducts around gas pipes may use 30 and 60 percent

practice.q: How often is calibration and shutdown tested?
a: State the frequency from the maintenance plan
Alarms also tested at set intervals

practice.q: What if a sensor is faulty?
a: Do not leave it inhibited without control

tip: Check no sensor is left inhibited after a test. It is an easy negative observation.

title: Cargo pump room fixed gas detection system
plain: Do officers know the pumproom gas detection, and is it working with calibrated sensors and correctly set alarms?
why: Pumproom leaks build up fast, so the alarms must work and be set low enough to give early warning.
checks: Company procedure for operation and maintenance
Control station fully working with no faults
Hydrocarbon alarm set point not higher than 10 percent LFL
Calibration records and span gas suitability
Alarms tested in pumproom, cargo control room and bridge
ready: Procedure with actions for alarm, low oxygen alarm and system failure
Manufacturer's manual
Maintenance and calibration records, monthly checks and after faults
In-date span gas
Manual atmosphere readings logged if the system was out of service
traps: No procedure for the system
Any hydrocarbon alarm above 10 percent LFL
Sensors not calibrated at the company frequency
Alarms in the cargo control room, pumproom or bridge not tested
Span gas expired or wrong
Sensors out of service, inhibited or disconnected
No manual readings while the system was out of service
say: Our pumproom system alarms no higher than 10 percent LFL and is calibrated and tested at the interval in our procedure. Alarms sound in the pumproom, cargo control room and bridge. If it fails we take manual readings and record them.

practice.q: What do you do when the pumproom gas alarm sounds?
a: Vacate the space and stop cargo pumps as set out

practice.q: What maintenance is done and when?
a: Visual inspection, alarm test and span gas check

practice.q: Do you check alarm levels when changing cargo?
a: Verify set points suit the cargo

tip: Exhaust duct sensors do not count for this question, so concentrate on the pumproom sensors.

title: Oxygen sensors in inert gas system spaces
plain: Do officers know the oxygen sensors and alarms in the inert gas plant space, and are they working, calibrated and set right?
why: Inert gas, CO2 or nitrogen can quietly remove oxygen, so the plant room must warn people before they collapse.
checks: Company procedure for the sensors and alarms
Control panel working with no faults
Alarm setting matches the company procedure
Calibration with proper span gas at the company frequency
Alarms tested at the company frequency
ready: Procedure with calibration interval, alarm values and actions on failure or low oxygen
Manufacturer's manual
Maintenance and calibration records
In-date span gas
Manual readings record for entry if sensors were out of service
traps: No procedure for the sensors and alarms
Sensors not calibrated at the company frequency
Audible or visual alarms not tested as required
Calibration gas out of date or unsuitable
Sensors out of service, inhibited or disconnected
No manual gas readings before and during entry when sensors were out of service
say: Our oxygen sensors in the inert gas plant space and their alarms are calibrated and tested at the company interval. I know the alarm values and what to do on a low oxygen alarm. If a sensor fails, we take manual readings before and during entry.

practice.q: At what oxygen level does the alarm activate?
a: Sensors alarm if oxygen falls below 19 percent
Visible and audible inside and outside the space

practice.q: What do you do on a low oxygen alarm?
a: Leave the space and keep others out

practice.q: What if the sensors fail?
a: Take manual readings before and during entry

tip: This applies to ships built from 2016 or older ships that fitted the sensors. Know which applies to yours.

title: Incident investigation reports for defined incidents
plain: Were all incidents reported and investigated, with a report or lessons learned bulletin for each serious one?
why: A ship only becomes safer if every incident is investigated and the lessons are shared with the crew.
checks: Incidents declared in the HVPQ and PIQ
A report or lessons learned bulletin onboard for each completed investigation
The onboard system for tracking incidents and near-misses
That no listed incident in the last 12 months is missing from the declaration
Inspector does not judge the quality of the report
ready: Company procedure for prompt reporting and investigation
Incident and near-miss tracking system
Investigation reports or lessons learned bulletins for each incident
Dates and status for ongoing investigations
List of incidents for the last 18 months
traps: No report or bulletin for an incident declared as completed
An incident in the last 12 months not declared in the HVPQ or PIQ
Not recognising an event as a defined incident
Investigation shown as ongoing without an expected date
say: All incidents and near-misses are reported and tracked under our SMS. For each defined incident we hold an investigation report or lessons learned bulletin. I can show the list and the documents.

practice.q: What events are counted as incidents?
a: Blackout, loss of propulsion or steering
Fire, flooding, spill over 1 cubic metre, lost time injury

practice.q: Where is the report for this incident?
a: Show it is in the tracking system

practice.q: How do you tell the crew the outcome?

tip: Include touching bottom, a breakaway from the berth and accommodation ladder hoisting wire failure. They are on the list.

title: Incident and near-miss reporting procedure
plain: Do crew know how to report incidents and near-misses, and can you show reports were investigated and closed out?
why: Near-misses show what could hurt someone next time, but only if everyone reports and follow-up happens.
checks: Company procedure for prompt reporting by all ranks
Two reports from the tracking system, in the right format
Reported to shore in the time limit and acknowledged
Investigated at the right level with corrective actions done
A rating asked how to report a near-miss
ready: Reporting and investigation procedure
Incident and near-miss tracking system
Reports from the last three months
Shore acknowledgements and investigation reports
Evidence outcomes were shared with the crew
traps: No procedure requiring reports from all ranks
Officer cannot explain tracking, reporting, investigating or closing out
Reports late or not acknowledged by shore
Corrective actions not carried out or closed out
No tracking system
Rating does not know how to report a near-miss
Outcome not shared with the crew
say: Anyone on board can report a near-miss under our SMS. Reports go to shore within the set time, are investigated at the right level and tracked until actions are closed. We share the outcome with the crew.

practice.q: What is a near-miss?
a: An event that could have caused loss but did not by chance
Includes unsafe conditions found after the danger passed
Report it even if nothing happened

practice.q: How do you report one?
a: Fill the form in our system
Goes to shore in the set time frame

practice.q: What happens after the report?

tip: If there were none in three months, be ready to state the date of the last near-miss report.

title: Shipboard safety meetings
plain: Do crew know how safety meetings are held and recorded, and did shore management answer the concerns raised?
why: Safety meetings give crew a voice, and shore response shows that problems get fixed.
checks: Company procedure for holding and recording meetings
Minutes for the last six months, one in detail
Roughly monthly meetings and an extra meeting after a serious incident or shore visit
Minutes sent to shore and shore response addressing issues
A rating asked if they attended and how they raise concerns
ready: Safety meeting procedure
Minutes in the company format with attendance
Proof minutes were submitted to shore
Shore responses and acknowledgements
Safety representative arrangement for those who cannot attend
traps: No procedure for meetings, minutes and shore review
Meetings not held about monthly or per the procedure
No extra meeting after a serious incident or shore visit
Minutes not in the right format or not sent to shore
Shore did not acknowledge or act on requests
Meeting held on the bridge at sea or at anchor, or in the CCR during cargo or tank cleaning
Rating does not know how to contribute
say: We hold safety meetings about monthly and after any serious incident. Minutes go to the office, which acknowledges them and responds to points needing help. Anyone who cannot attend can pass concerns through the safety representative.

practice.q: How often do you hold safety meetings?
a: At the interval in our SMS, about monthly
Extra meeting after a serious incident
Also during shore management visits where practical

practice.q: How can you raise a concern if you miss the meeting?
a: Concern goes to the safety committee

practice.q: How do you know shore saw the minutes?

tip: Hold meetings in the mess or a meeting room. Meetings on the bridge at sea or in the CCR during cargo are a finding. Do not use them for training.
refs: MCA Code of Safe Working Practices

title: Work planning procedure
plain: Do crew know the work planning procedure, and are planning meetings held and recorded as required?
why: Planning the work together avoids clashes, missed permits and unsafe surprises.
checks: Company procedure for documented work planning meetings
Several meeting records from the last month
Records follow the company format, approved onboard, and match what the ship did
A task needing a permit or risk assessment has the document
A rating asked where to find today's plan
ready: Work planning procedure
Daily plan records for the previous month
Permits, risk assessments and detailed work plans referenced in the plan
Evidence of shore approval where needed
Plan available in the place ratings know
traps: No procedure for documented work planning
Meetings not held at the required frequency
Records not approved or not in the correct format
Not enough detail to understand the job
Planned tasks needed permits or risk assessments but none available
Plan does not match the real work of the ship
Shore approval needed but not shown
Rating does not know where the plan is
say: We hold a work planning meeting as per our SMS, usually daily, with those doing the work. The record shows tasks, permits, risk assessments, PPE, supervisors and any shore approval, and it is approved onboard. Any new task is added and communicated before work starts.

practice.q: What is covered in the work planning meeting?
a: Scope of work and conflicts between departments
People, tools, PPE and rest hours

practice.q: What if an unplanned job comes up?
a: Review and update the plan record
Tell those who will do the job

practice.q: Where do you find today's plan?

tip: Make sure each task on the plan says whether a permit is needed and then keep that permit with the plan.

title: Stop Work Authority
plain: Does everyone know they can stop unsafe work, and how to do it, without being blamed?
why: A single person speaking up can stop an accident before it happens.
checks: Company Stop Work Authority policy and procedure
Three to five crew members questioned at random
Stop Work Authority mentioned in toolbox talks, risk assessments, planning and safety meetings
Inspector will not test crew by committing unsafe acts
If a crew member stops work during the inspection, work stops
ready: Company Stop Work Authority policy and procedure
Toolbox talk and planning meeting records that mention it
Safety meeting minutes covering it
Shared understanding of how to give the stop instruction clearly
Knowledge of the five steps
traps: No Stop Work Authority policy or procedure
No evidence it is included in planning, risk assessments or meetings
More than one crew member does not know the policy
say: Anyone on board, including contractors, has the right and duty to stop unsafe work. We stop the activity, tell the person in charge, discuss and fix the issue, then restart and share what we learned. No one is blamed for using it.

practice.q: What would you do if you saw unsafe work?

a: Even if the danger turns out not to be real
Company supports it at all levels

practice.q: How do you give the stop instruction?
a: Clear and direct so it is not misunderstood

tip: Mention Stop Work Authority at every toolbox talk. Ratings are asked in the inspection, and more than one wrong answer is a finding.
